questions.q: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
questions.solution: The ammonium ion is \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) and the carbonate ion is \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\). Two ammonium ions balance one carbonate ion, giving \(\mathrm{(NH_{4})_{2}CO_{3}}\). (Ammonia, \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\), is the neutral molecule, not the ion.)

questions.q: Which species contains a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond?
questions.solution: In \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) the lone pair on the nitrogen of ammonia is donated to an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion, so both electrons of that bond come from one atom. Once formed, the four N–H bonds are identical. Ammonia and water have lone pairs but no dative bond. (Having a lone pair is not the same as having a dative bond.)

questions.q: The ions \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) all have the electron configuration \(\mathrm{1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}}\). Which list puts them in order of increasing ionic radius?
questions.solution: The ions are isoelectronic: each has 10 electrons. The nuclear charge rises from 8 (oxygen) to 12 (magnesium), so the same electrons are pulled in more tightly and the radius falls. Smallest to largest: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+} < Na^{+} < F^{-} < O^{2-}}\). (Ordering by the size of the charge alone puts \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) first.)

questions.q: Which compound has the strongest ionic bonding?
questions.solution: Ionic bonding is stronger when the ions have larger charges and smaller radii, so their centres are closer. MgO and CaO both have 2+ and 2− ions, and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) is smaller than \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\), so MgO has the strongest bonding. (CaO is the close miss: the right charges, but a larger cation.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium?

options.A: Magnesium ions have a larger charge and are smaller, and each atom contributes two delocalised electrons, so the metallic bonding is stronger.
options.B: Magnesium atoms have more protons, so the covalent bonds between the atoms are stronger.
options.C: Magnesium has a giant ionic lattice, while sodium has a giant metallic lattice.
options.D: Magnesium has stronger intermolecular forces because its atoms have more electrons.

questions.solution: Both are giant metallic lattices. \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ions have twice the charge of \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), are smaller, and are surrounded by twice as many delocalised electrons per ion, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger and more energy is needed to melt the metal. (Metals have no covalent bonds or intermolecular forces between atoms.)

questions.q: A solid melts at \(1710\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\). It does not conduct electricity when solid or when molten, and it is insoluble in water. What type of structure does it have?
questions.solution: A very high melting point means a giant structure with strong bonds throughout. It cannot be ionic, which conducts when molten, or metallic, which conducts when solid. Simple molecular solids melt at low temperatures. So it is giant covalent, like silicon dioxide. (Ionic solids also have high melting points, but molten ionic compounds conduct.)

questions.q: Which statement explains why graphite conducts electricity?

options.A: The layers can slide over each other, carrying charge with them.
options.B: Graphite contains ions that are free to move between the layers.
options.C: Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move along the layers.
options.D: The weak forces between the layers allow electrons to jump from one layer to the next.

questions.solution: In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to three others in a flat hexagonal layer. Its fourth outer electron is delocalised over the layer, and these electrons move along the layers when a potential difference is applied. (Sliding layers explain why graphite is soft, not why it conducts.)

questions.q: What are the shape of the oxonium ion, \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\), and its H–O–H bond angle?
questions.solution: The oxygen has four electron pairs: three bonding pairs and one lone pair (oxygen's six outer electrons, plus three from the hydrogens, minus one for the positive charge). Like ammonia, the ion is pyramidal. The lone pair repels more than the bonding pairs, closing the angle to \(107^{\circ}\). (Counting only the three bonds leads to trigonal planar.)

questions.q: What is the shape of a xenon tetrafluoride molecule, \(\mathrm{XeF_{4}}\)?
questions.solution: Xenon has eight outer electrons. Four form bonds to fluorine, leaving two lone pairs: six electron pairs in all, arranged octahedrally. The two lone pairs sit opposite each other to minimise repulsion, so the four F atoms form a square planar molecule with \(90^{\circ}\) angles. (Ignoring the lone pairs leads to tetrahedral.)

questions.q: Methane, \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\), has a bond angle of \(109.5^{\circ}\), and water has a smaller bond angle. Which statement best explains why?

options.A: Water has two lone pairs, which repel more strongly than bonding pairs and push the O–H bonds closer together.
options.B: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the hydrogen atoms closer together.
options.C: Water has only two bonds, so there is less repulsion between them.
options.D: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules pull the hydrogen atoms together.

questions.solution: Both have four electron pairs around the central atom. In water two of them are lone pairs, which are held closer to the oxygen and repel more strongly than bonding pairs (lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair). This squeezes the H–O–H angle to about \(104.5^{\circ}\). (Counting only the two bonds and ignoring the lone pairs would predict a linear molecule.)

questions.q: Which is the meaning of electronegativity?

options.A: The energy released when an atom gains an electron
options.B: The energy needed to remove an electron from an atom
options.C: The attraction between a nucleus and its outer electrons
options.D: The power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond

questions.solution: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. It has no unit and is measured on the Pauling scale. The first two options describe electron affinity and ionisation energy. (Electronegativity is about a shared pair in a bond, not about gaining or losing electrons.)

questions.q: Which molecule has a permanent dipole?
questions.solution: All four contain polar bonds. In \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) (linear), \(\mathrm{BF_{3}}\) (trigonal planar) and \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) (tetrahedral) the identical bonds are arranged symmetrically, so their dipoles cancel. In \(\mathrm{CHCl_{3}}\) one C–Cl is replaced by C–H, so the dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar. (Polar bonds alone do not make a polar molecule.)

questions.q: Which substance forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules in the liquid?
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonding needs a hydrogen atom bonded directly to N, O or F, and a lone pair on N, O or F in a neighbouring molecule. Only methanol has an O–H bond. In fluoromethane and methoxymethane the hydrogens are bonded to carbon, and chlorine is not electronegative enough. (Containing O or F is not enough: the H must be bonded to it.)

questions.q: The boiling points of the hydrogen halides increase from HCl to HBr to HI. Which statement best explains this trend?

options.A: The molecules have more electrons, so the London (induced dipole) forces between them get stronger.
options.B: The permanent dipoles get stronger as the halogen gets larger.
options.C: Hydrogen bonding between the molecules gets stronger down the group.
options.D: The H–X bond gets stronger, so more energy is needed to boil the compound.

questions.solution: Down the group the halogen has more electrons, so larger temporary dipoles form and London forces increase. The permanent dipoles actually get weaker, because electronegativity falls. Boiling separates molecules and breaks no covalent bonds. (HF is the one with hydrogen bonding, which is why it boils highest of all.)

questions.q: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane both have the formula \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}}\). Pentane boils at \(36\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\) and 2,2-dimethylpropane at \(10\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\). Which statement best explains the difference?

options.A: 2,2-dimethylpropane has fewer electrons, so its London forces are weaker.
options.B: The branched molecules are more compact and have less surface contact, so the London forces between them are weaker.
options.C: Branched molecules have weaker C–C bonds, which break more easily on boiling.
options.D: Pentane molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, but 2,2-dimethylpropane molecules cannot.

questions.solution: The two isomers have the same number of electrons. The branched molecule is roughly spherical, so neighbouring molecules touch over a smaller area, fewer induced dipole attractions form, and less energy is needed to separate them. No covalent bonds break when a liquid boils. (Neither alkane can form hydrogen bonds.)

questions.q: Which statement explains why ice is less dense than liquid water?

options.A: The covalent bonds in ice are longer than those in liquid water.
options.B: Ice contains trapped air between its molecules.
options.C: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice in which they are further apart than in the liquid.
options.D: There are no hydrogen bonds in ice, so the molecules move further apart.

questions.solution: In ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four others in a regular, open, tetrahedral lattice. In the liquid some of these bonds break and the molecules pack more closely, so the same mass occupies less volume. (Ice has more hydrogen bonds than water, not fewer.)

questions.q: Iodine sublimes on gentle heating, forming a purple vapour of \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) molecules. What is overcome when iodine sublimes?
questions.solution: Solid iodine is a simple molecular lattice of \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) molecules held together by London forces. On sublimation the molecules separate, but each I–I covalent bond stays intact: the vapour is still \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\). (If the covalent bonds broke, the vapour would be iodine atoms.)

questions.q: Ethanol mixes completely with water, but hexane does not. Which statement best explains this?

options.A: Ethanol and water are both covalent, but hexane is ionic.
options.B: Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane can only form London forces, which are too weak to make up for the hydrogen bonds it would break between water molecules.
options.C: Hexane molecules are too large to fit between water molecules.
options.D: Hexane reacts with water to form an insoluble layer.

questions.solution: For a liquid to dissolve, the new attractions formed must compensate for those broken. Ethanol's O–H group forms hydrogen bonds with water. Hexane would break water's hydrogen bonds but form only weak London forces in return, so it stays as a separate layer. (Hexane is a covalent molecule and does not react with water.)

questions.q: Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds in ethane, ethene and ethyne is correct?

options.A: The C–C single bond is the shortest and the strongest.
options.B: All three bonds have the same length, but different strengths.
options.C: The C≡C triple bond is the shortest and the strongest.
options.D: The C≡C triple bond is the longest, because it contains the most electrons.

questions.solution: More shared pairs between the two nuclei give a stronger attraction, which pulls the nuclei closer. So bond length falls and bond strength rises from C–C to C=C to C≡C: the triple bond is the shortest and the strongest. (More electrons in the bond pull the atoms together, not apart.)

questions.q: How many lone pairs of electrons are there on the bromine atom in bromine pentafluoride, \(\mathrm{BrF_{5}}\)?
questions.solution: Bromine has 7 outer electrons. Five of them form single bonds with the five fluorine atoms, leaving 2 electrons: one lone pair. Six electron pairs in all give a square pyramidal molecule, so the number of lone pairs on bromine = 1. (Assuming every outer electron of bromine is used in bonding leads to 0.)
